text:

On October 13, 2023, we completed our acquisition of Activision Blizzard for a total purchase price of $75.4 billion, consisting primarily of cash.[1] This is stated in the FY2024 10-K (fiscal year ended June 30, 2024).

A separate figure appears in the 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2023: On October 13, 2023, we completed our acquisition of Activision Blizzard, Inc. for a cash payment of $61.8 billion, net of cash acquired.[2]

queries.query: clients moving cash into higher-yielding products, cash sweep, net interest revenue
net interest revenue decline from clients moving cash into higher-yielding investments

text:
Charles Schwab's FY2023 10-K said that as a result of rapidly increasing short-term interest rates beginning in 2022, the Company saw an increase in the pace at which clients moved certain cash balances out of our sweep features and into higher-yielding alternatives at Schwab.[1] In its MD&A, the company said net interest revenue fell because of this shift, as net interest revenue decreased $1.3 billion, or 12%, in 2023 from 2022 primarily due to increased utilization of higher-cost supplemental funding sources to support client cash allocations in the rising rate environment, and lower average interest-earning assets, which more than offset the benefits of higher average yields on interest-earning assets.[2]

Key details from the filing:

- **Pace of cash movement:** The average pace of client cash allocations out of sweep products into higher-yielding investment solutions decreased significantly beginning in the second quarter of 2023, and, apart from an increase in August following the Federal Reserve's July rate increase, continued to decline during the second half of 2023.[3]
- **Interest-earning assets:** Average interest-earning assets for 2023 were lower by 21% compared to 2022, which was primarily due to lower bank deposits and payables to brokerage clients as a result of clients allocating cash out of sweep products into higher-yielding investment solutions due to higher market interest rates.[4]
- **Funding:** To support this client cash allocation activity, the Company has been utilizing temporary supplemental funding beginning in the fourth quarter of 2022 and throughout 2023, including drawing upon FHLB secured lending facilities and issuing brokered CDs.[5]
- **Margin:** Despite the revenue decline, net interest margin increased to 1.98% in 2023, from 1.78% in 2022, as higher market interest rates improved yields on interest-earning assets, which more than offset the higher rates paid across interest-bearing funding sources.[6]
- **Outlook:** While client cash realignment activity has slowed significantly since the second quarter of 2023, continued uncertainty remains, including in regard to the path of market interest rates and client behavior, which will significantly impact our utilization of supplemental funding sources.[7]

queries.query: July 2024 Falcon sensor update incident outage customers

text:
CrowdStrike said the July 19, 2024 incident was caused by a Falcon sensor update and has had, and is expected to keep having, an adverse effect on its business. In its FY2025 10-K (year ended January 31, 2025), the company released a content configuration update for its Falcon sensor that resulted in system crashes for certain Windows systems (the "July 19 Incident")[1], and the July 19 Incident has had, and is expected to continue to have, an adverse effect on our business, sales, customer and partner relations, reputation, results of operations and financial condition.[2]

**Costs and remediation (10-K FY2025 risk factors):**
- It has incurred, and expects to continue to incur, significant costs and expenses related to the incident, including in connection with remediation efforts, customer and partner relations, measures taken to address the damage to our reputation, and other measures taken in response to the incident.[3]
- While it is investing in enhancements to software resiliency, testing and customer controls following the July 19 Incident, it cannot guarantee that such enhancements will be effective, or that our products do not have or will not have defects, errors, or vulnerabilities.[4]

**Customers, partners and competitors (10-K FY2025 risk factors):**
- Certain of its existing or prospective customers have elected to, and may in the future elect to, defer purchasing decisions relating to its products and services or not purchase its products and services at all.[5]
- Customers have also decided, and may in the future decide, to terminate or not renew their agreements with it.[6]
- The incident has negatively impacted, and may in the future negatively impact, existing or prospective partners' ability or willingness to promote its products or services.[7]
- Certain competitors have aggressively approached current and prospective customers and partners to attempt to capitalize on the incident, and may continue to do so.[8]
- It has agreed to, and expects to agree to in the future, provide incentives in connection with its commercial arrangements with customers, including subscription period extensions, discounts or promotional modules.[9]

**Legal and financial effects (10-K FY2025 MD&A):**
- As a result of the July 19 Incident, it is subject to lawsuits, claims and inquiries as described in Note 10, Commitments and Contingencies, in Part II, Item 8 of this Annual Report on Form 10-K.[10]
- It is not reasonably possible to quantify the precise impact of the July 19 Incident, but the incident has adversely affected our results of operations, and it currently expects a number of factors relating to the incident to adversely affect our key metrics and results of operations in future periods.[11]
- While it has maintained high dollar-based gross retention rates following the incident, it has experienced delays in creating sales opportunities and longer sales cycles, including delays in customer purchasing decisions.[12]
- Customer commitment packages introduced following the July 19 Incident have included discounting, additional modules, professional services, flexible payment terms or subscription period extensions.[13]
- Its customer commitment packages have resulted, and are expected to continue to result, in increased contraction, due to elongated subscription terms, and decreased upsell dollar values.[14]

**Later 10-Q wording:** In the 10-Q for the quarter ended October 31, 2025, the company said that sales cycles may be elongated in future periods.[15] Its earlier 10-Q for the quarter ended October 31, 2024 said that while it had not experienced high levels of customer churn following the incident, it had experienced delays in creating sales opportunities and longer sales cycles, including delays in customer purchasing decisions.[16]

docs.title: CRWD 10-K FY2025 (year ended 2025-01-31), Item 1A Risk Factors

text:
JNJ said it is a defendant in numerous lawsuits over talc, and it recorded a large talc-related charge and reserve in fiscal 2023. The Company is a defendant in numerous lawsuits arising out of the use of body powders containing talc, primarily JOHNSON'S Baby Powder, and the Company's sale, manufacturing and marketing of opioids.[1]

Key points from the FY2023 10-K (year ended December 31, 2023):

- **Defense and uncertainty:** While the Company believes it has substantial defenses in these matters, it is not feasible to predict the ultimate outcome of litigation.[2]
- **Potential exposure:** The Company could in the future be required to pay significant amounts as a result of settlements or judgments in these matters, potentially in excess of accruals, including matters where the Company could be held jointly and severally liable among other defendants.[3]
- **Charge:** Fiscal 2023 includes an approximately $7.0 billion charge related to talc matters[4]. The MD&A's other income and expense discussion says 2023 was primarily related to the approximately $7.0 billion charge for talc[5].
- **Reserve and liquidity:** The company said its operating cash flows and other sources would provide sufficient resources to fund operating needs, including the establishment of the approximately $9 billion reserve for talc matters[6].

queries.query: higher interest rates increase financing costs on variable rate debt and refinancing
higher interest rates reduce property values and real estate valuations, cap rates

text:
Across the FY2023 filings, REITs most often said that higher interest rates would raise their borrowing costs and could reduce property valuations. These statements are risk-factor warnings, not reported outcomes, except where a filing says rates had already increased its costs.

**Financing costs**
- Simon Property Group (10-K, FY2023) said that when interest rates increase, then so does the interest costs on our unhedged variable rate debt, which could adversely affect our cash flows[1].
- UDR (10-K, FY2023) said that we have experienced increases in the interest rates on such indebtedness, which has increased our interest expense and adversely impacted our results of operations and cash flows.[2]
- Ventas (10-K, FY2023) said that an increase in or elevated interest rates also could limit our ability to refinance existing debt upon maturity or cause us to pay higher rates upon refinancing[3].
- Regency Centers (10-K, FY2023) said that higher interest rates adversely impact our cost of borrowing.[4]

As of December 31, 2023, we had approximately $479.7 million of variable rate indebtedness outstanding, which constitutes approximately 8.3% of total outstanding indebtedness as of such date, and we have experienced increases in the interest rates on such indebtedness, which has increased our interest expense and adversely impacted our results of operations and cash flows.

Additionally, higher interest rates adversely impact our cost of borrowing.

To the extent the current high interest rate environment continues or interest rates increase further, we could experience higher interest expense on our variable-rate debt or increase interest rates when refinancing maturing fixed-rate debt, which could have a material adverse effect on us and our ability to make payments on our debt and to make distributions or cause us to be in default under certain debt instruments.

Increases in interest rates could have a material adverse effect on our cost of capital, and our decision to hedge against interest rate risk might not be effective The current high interest rate environment has been increasing interest cost on new and existing variable rate debt.

In addition, in an elevated interest rate environment, new debt, whether fixed or variable, is likely to be more expensive than debt that is being refinanced, which could, among other things, make the financing of any acquisition or investment more expensive, and we may be unable to incur new debt or replace maturing debt with new debt at equal or better interest rates.

Historically, during periods of increasing interest rates, real estate valuations have generally decreased as a result of rising capitalization rates which tend to move directionally with interest rates.

Combined with high interest rates and reduced market liquidity, this may result in a prolonged period of reduced property valuations and increased capitalization rates, potentially necessitating the recognition of additional significant real estate impairments.
Increases in or elevated interest rates may result in a decrease in the value of our real estate, a decrease in the market price of our common stock and a decrease in our cash flows and net income.

Prolonged periods of higher interest rates may negatively impact the valuation of our real estate asset portfolio and could result in a decline of our stock price and market capitalization, which may adversely impact our ability and willingness to raise equity capital on favorable terms through sales of our common shares, including through our At the Market ("ATM") program.
Higher interest rates also increased and could continue to increase capitalization rates, which may lead to reduced valuations of the Company’s assets.

Higher interest rates may also lead purchasers of our common stock to demand a greater annual dividend yield, which could adversely affect the market price of our common stock and could result in increased capitalization rates, which may lead to reduced valuation of our assets.

In addition, an increase in interest rates could decrease the amounts third-parties are willing to pay for our assets, thereby limiting our ability to change our portfolio promptly in response to changes in economic or other conditions.

In NVIDIA's fiscal 2022 10-K (year ended January 30, 2022), the China export risk was described in general terms. The increasing focus on the strategic importance of AI technologies may result in additional regulatory restrictions that target products and services capable of enabling or facilitating AI, including some or all of our product and service offerings. Such restrictions could limit our ability to serve demand abroad and could negatively impact our business and financial results.[1] By fiscal 2024 (year ended January 28, 2024), NVIDIA named specific products and restrictions. AMD's fiscal 2022 10-K (year ended December 31, 2022) cited one specific China product restriction, and its fiscal 2024 10-K (year ended December 28, 2024) described controls on named products and a pre-shipment notification process.

**NVIDIA, fiscal 2022 (year ended January 30, 2022)**
- Geopolitical tensions could lead to changing regulatory requirements, trade policies, export controls, import duties and economic disruptions[2], which NVIDIA said could affect its operations and profitability.
- It described the risk of restrictions into Russia[3] and said that we recently ceased product sales to Russia.[4]
- It warned that our inability to sell to a customer due to U.S. trade restrictions[5] could harm its financial condition.

**NVIDIA, fiscal 2024 (year ended January 28, 2024)**
- The USG restrictions targeted China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and Russia, and specifically impact our A100 and H100 integrated circuits[6].
- NVIDIA said that we have not received licenses to ship these restricted products to China.[7]
- It also said that we transitioned some operations, including certain testing, validation, and supply and distribution operations out of China and Hong Kong.[8]
- It said the USG is evaluating license requests in a closed process that does not have clear standards or an opportunity for review.[9]
- It warned that export controls may disrupt our supply and distribution chain for a substantial portion of our products, which are warehoused in and distributed from Hong Kong.[10]

**AMD, fiscal 2022 (year ended December 31, 2022)**
- AMD said that BIS has issued new requirements that prevent us from shipping MI250 and MI250X integrated circuits to China and Russia without a license.[11]
- It said that United States-China trade relations remain uncertain as the United States continues to add more Chinese companies to the Entity List and more regulations targeted to advanced computing, semiconductor manufacturing, and AI.[12]

**AMD, fiscal 2024 (year ended December 28, 2024)**
- AMD said that these controls prevent us from shipping certain AMD Instinct™ integrated circuits and certain AMD Versal™ FPGAs to China, or to customers outside of the United States whose ultimate parent is headquartered in a D5 country (including China), without a license.[13]
- It said that these controls also require us to file a Notified Advanced Computing (NAC) notification with BIS 25 days before shipping certain Versal FPGAs to China[14].
- It noted that the NAC notification process could result in BIS prohibiting a shipment or requiring a license application before shipping a product that is the subject of a NAC notification.[15]

Not in the passages found: NVIDIA's specific China product restrictions for fiscal 2022.

The loss of any of our large customers, a significant reduction in purchases by them, our inability to sell to a customer due to U.S. trade restrictions, or any difficulties in collecting accounts receivable would likely harm our financial condition and results of operations.

These restrictions impact exports of certain chips, as well as software, hardware, equipment and technology used to develop, produce and manufacture certain chips to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and Russia, and specifically impact our A100 and H100 integrated circuits, DGX or any other systems or boards which incorporate A100 or H100 integrated circuits.
